sections.title: What changes the load on your knees
sections.text: Squat depth, step height, balance, speed, resistance and jumping impact all change how hard your knees work. There is no universal rule that your knee must never move past your toes. How far your knee can comfortably travel differs between people and between tasks.

sections.title: Practical swaps
sections.text: A controlled sit-to-stand, a supported split squat or a low step-up can be easier to learn than a fast jump squat. A shallower or slower version may feel more comfortable in some cases. When impact is a problem, low-impact conditioning such as cycling or walking on level ground can work better than jumping.

sections.title: Build up gradually
sections.text: Start with a movement and an amount of training your knees tolerate. Add load, depth or reps only while symptoms stay acceptable during and after training. Don’t keep testing a painful position to see whether it has “fixed itself.” General exercise advice is not a diagnosis or a rehab program.

sections.title: When to get help
sections.text: A very painful, visibly deformed or badly swollen knee, being unable to put weight on it, locking, fever with redness, or symptoms after a significant injury need prompt professional assessment. Problems that persist should be checked too.

sections.title: Using TrainUp
sections.text: Add your knees as a limitation in Profile, with a note, and set whether jumping is OK. The plan then leaves out exercises that don’t fit. If an exercise hurts, “I feel pain” ends it and keeps it out of your plans until you resume it from Profile. No exercise is guaranteed to be “knee-safe” for everyone.
